8.3.1 Long Spur Ridge Site
The Long Spur Ridge pumped storage site is located on Thompson River in Transylvania County, North Carolina, about 2.8 miles southwest of Oakland, and about 2.7 miles northeast of the Bad Creek site. The Long Spur Ridge site is located within the Nantahala National Forest (Figure 8-1).
The Jocassee Reservoir would form the lower reservoir of the project, and the steep slope of the Thompson River would provide the opportunity of high head pumped storage development. The upper reservoir would contain a usable storage capacity of 26,000 acre-feet between elevations 2,700 and 2,570 feet. At the maximum elevation, the reservoir area would be 280 acres. The upper dam would have a maximum height of about 350 feet with a crest length of about 2,700 feet. The power tunnel would be 34 feet in diameter, and its total length would be about 14,500 feet. Four units rated at 250 MW each would be installed in an underground powerhouse, unless the geological conditions would not permit such construction.
8.3.1.1 Flora
The Thompson River Gorge supports vegetation similar to that described in Subsection 2.2.1. The mixed mesophytic forest community located on flood plains or in deep moist coves is richer in species than any other gorge community, often including 25 tree species with no single dominant. Common tree species include eastern hemlock, Fraser magnolia, white basswood, white oak, yellow poplar, sweet birch (Betula lenta), and butternut (Juglans cinerea) (Mowbray and Oosting, 1968).
The adverse impacts to vegetation expected from construction and operation of the Long Spur Ridge site are similar in kind to those discussed in Subsections 3.1.2 and 3.2.2, although the area is smaller. Approximately 280 acres of riverbank shrub thicket, disturbed floodplain forest, mixed mesophytic forest, and mixed oak-hickory forest would be inundated by formation of the upper reservoir. Also adversely affected would be the vegetative communities in the borrow and spoil areas, transmission line right-of-way, and other areas used for construction activities. The associated wildlife habitat, wildlife, timber, and watershed values of these forested areas would also be lost.
